mean: nothing in this world lasts forever
lit: all things that come into being are without permanence

story.text: A core Buddhist teaching: everything that arises from causes keeps changing and passes away, so nothing can be held on to. Japanese readers know it best from the opening lines of The Tale of the Heike, which recounts the fall of the once all-powerful Taira clan: the bell of the Gion monastery rings with the sound of 'all things are impermanent'.
story.source: Buddhist teaching; opening of 『平家物語』

near.diff: 栄枯盛衰 is the rise and fall of people, families or businesses; 諸行無常 is the wider truth that every thing passes away.

mean: good rewarded and evil punished, as in old tales
lit: encourage the good, chastise the wicked

story.text: The idea comes from the Zuo Zhuan, which praises the Spring and Autumn Annals for the way their wording 'punishes evil and encourages good'. In Japan it became the label for moral fiction, above all the Edo-period novel 'Nansō Satomi Hakkenden' by Kyokutei Bakin, and today for any story in which the villain is always defeated.

story.text: The Records of the Grand Historian tell of the man who drove the chariot of Yanzi, prime minister of Qi. His wife watched him through the gate: under the great canopy, whipping four horses, he looked triumphant and very pleased with himself. That evening she asked to leave him, saying the prime minister himself looked humble while he, a mere driver, was so full of himself. The driver changed his ways, and Yanzi, learning why, made him an official.

意気投合 is hitting it off with someone; 意気揚々 is one's own triumphant mood.

mean: sharing the same fate, for better or worse
lit: entrusting one's rebirth to the same single lotus

story.text: In Pure Land Buddhism, those who are saved are reborn after death in paradise, seated on lotus flowers. The phrase first meant being reborn there together on one and the same lotus. In everyday Japanese it came to mean that people are tied to one outcome, now often a bad one: if one falls, they all fall.

The Chinese phrase 'one day, three autumns' grew in Japanese into 'one day, a thousand autumns', the longing of someone who can hardly bear to wait.

mean: the greatest attempt of one's whole life
lit: once in one's whole life and generation

story.text: Originally a term of the noh and kabuki stage: an actor, usually before retiring, would perform one of his famous roles for the last time as the crowning performance of his career. From this it came to mean the biggest, once-in-a-lifetime undertaking of anyone's life.

use.how: 一世一代の + noun: 大勝負, 決断, プロポーズ, 晴れ舞台. Said of a person's own single, biggest act or occasion.

near.diff: 一発勝負 is any contest settled in one try; 一世一代 is the biggest undertaking of a whole lifetime.

cue: After years of saving and nerves, he kneels in front of everyone at the restaurant and opens the ring box. What kind of proposal is it?
